title: Why they studied the sky
hook: prayer times, the qiblah and the new moon made astronomy a devotion

segments.voice: Yesterday, the astrolabe: a brass instrument for finding the hour and the direction of prayer by the stars. Your line was: the stars tell the time. Did you find north last night? Day nine hundred twenty-seven.

The prayers come through the day, but when, exactly? Not by a clock on the wall. By the sun. The Qur'an puts it plainly, in Pickthall's translation: "worship at fixed hours hath been enjoined on the believers." Fixed hours, read from shadows, from sunset, from the last light in the west. Then a direction to face, from wherever you happen to be standing. Then a month that begins only when someone sees a thin crescent after sunset. Questions about the sky, and not idle ones. They come from the prayer mat and the fast.
screen: `WORSHIP AT FIXED HOURS.` → `A DIRECTION TO FACE.` → `A MONTH THAT STARTS WITH A CRESCENT.`

segments.voice: Start with the moon. People asked the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, about the new moons, and the Qur'an answers, in Pickthall's words: "They are fixed seasons for mankind and for the pilgrimage." The crescent opens each month, so it opens Ramadan, the pilgrimage season and the feasts. Bukhari records the Prophet's instruction: fast when you see it, stop fasting when you see it again, and if clouds hide it, complete the month as thirty days. The calendar rests on a human eye, looking west at dusk. Then the direction. The Qur'an tells believers to turn their faces toward the Sacred Mosque wherever they are. Near Mecca, you can almost point. Far away, on a round earth, finding that line takes geometry: angles, distances, the shape of the globe. Then the hours. Tirmidhi records a report in which the angel Gabriel leads the Prophet in prayer at set moments: when the sun passes its height, when a shadow has grown, when the sun goes down, when the twilight fades. Every one of those is something you see in the sky or on the ground. So the sky became homework. The astrolabe makers you met yesterday were working on questions that started at the mosque door. And the conversation hasn't stopped. Muslims today settle the new moon in more than one way: some communities wait for a sighting in their own sky, some accept a sighting from another country, and some rely on calculation. Each reads the Prophet's instruction in its own way, and each is trying to keep the same fast. Science for prayer.
screen: `FIXED SEASONS FOR MANKIND.` · `TURN YOUR FACE, WHEREVER YOU ARE.` · `SHADOWS AND SUNSETS MARK THE HOURS.` · `ONE HADITH, SEVERAL WAYS TO SIGHT.` · then, large: `SCIENCE FOR PRAYER.`

segments.voice: The practice: get ready to watch for the new moon. Settle, and breathe. A new crescent shows low and thin in the sky where the sun has just gone down, in the short while after sunset. Make a note to find out what time the sun sets where you are tonight, so you know when to look. For now, notice the light where you are right now: how bright it is, which way the shadows fall, how long they are. People read the hour from exactly that. If you pray, you can let this quiet be part of waiting for the next prayer. If you don't, just keep watching the light. The bell holds the time.
Mawaqit, appointed times: the Qur'an's word for the fixed hours of prayer, one of the sky questions, with the direction of prayer and the new moon, that sent people to the stars. Today's word.
Your line: science for prayer. Today, step outside once around sunset and look west, even for ten seconds, and see what the sky is doing. Day nine hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims begin Ramadan and the other months by the new crescent, set prayer times by the sun's position, and face the qiblah toward Mecca; communities differ on whether the crescent must be seen locally or may be accepted from elsewhere or by calculation.

original.note: Arabic: appointed times, the word Pickthall renders "fixed seasons" in 2:189.

trapdoor: what you thought: astronomy was a hobby that happened to sit beside religion.
what it means: prayer times, the direction of prayer and the new moon all depend on the sky, so worship handed astronomers their daily questions.
what a scholar hears: mawaqit, appointed times, in 2:189, and a calendar that hangs on a crescent seen with the eye at dusk.

notes: Pickthall 4:103 and 2:189 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording (4:103 begins 'Lo! worship at fixed hours...').
Hadith numbers Bukhari 1909 and Tirmidhi 149 should be confirmed against the standard numbering.
The Gabriel hadith's markers are summarized loosely (sun passing its height, shadow length, sunset, end of twilight); confirm the summary.
The three approaches to the new moon (local sighting, accepting sightings elsewhere, calculation) are described without ranking; confirm fair.
'Far away, on a round earth, finding that line takes geometry' is a general statement; the index hook's 'made astronomy a devotion' is softened to 'questions from worship'.

Editor: replaced the 'turn toward the west' practice (too close to yesterday's 'turn toward north') with checking tonight's sunset time; changed 'scholars with astrolabes and tables you met this past week' to what the path actually covered (yesterday's astrolabe); softened 'each gives reasons from the same hadith' to 'each reads the Prophet's instruction in its own way'.

Auditor: 'when the red of twilight fades' changed to 'when the twilight fades' (the hadith says the shafaq disappears; schools differ on whether shafaq is the red or the white glow); dropped the stock 'Today: ...' hook ending.
